1.title: Escalation and Error Propagation
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Escalation and Error Propagation. This module covers task statements five point two and five point three: escalation and error propagation. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. The right escalation triggers, and why sentiment and self-reported confidence are poor proxies. What to do on an explicit request for a human, on frustration, on policy gaps and on multiple matches. Structured error context for multi-agent recovery. The two anti-patterns: silent suppression and total abort.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply's Agent Escalates the Wrong Cases
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply's Agent Escalates the Wrong Cases. The target is eighty percent plus first-contact resolution, but the agent reaches only sixty-two percent. It escalates routine address changes on unshipped orders and tries to handle alone gift-card disputes that need policy exceptions.

1.title: When to escalate
1.text: When to escalate. The customer explicitly asks for a human. Honor it immediately, without first investigating. Policy has an exception or a gap. The policy is silent or ambiguous about the request (for example, a price match against a competitor when policy covers only your own site). The agent cannot make meaningful progress. Repeated failed attempts, missing access.

1.title: When to escalate, continued
1.text: When to escalate, continued. The customer sounds frustrated. Acknowledge the frustration and offer to resolve if it is within the agent's capability; escalate if the customer repeats the wish for a person. The case looks complex. Complexity alone is not the criterion; policy gaps and inability to progress are.

1.title: When to escalate, continued
1.text: When to escalate, continued. The figure shows this: Escalation decisions: honor explicit requests at once, escalate for policy gaps or lack of progress, otherwise resolve; ask for identifiers when matches are ambiguous.

1.title: Unreliable proxies
1.text: Unreliable proxies. Sentiment analysis measures mood, not case complexity: a calm customer can have a policy-exception case and an angry one a simple fix. Self-reported confidence scores (one to ten) are poorly calibrated: the agent is often confidently wrong on exactly the hard cases. Fix the root cause (unclear decision boundaries) with explicit escalation criteria and few-shot examples in the system prompt, showing when to escalate and when to resolve alone. Training a separate classifier is over-engineered before prompt optimization has been tried.

1.title: Ambiguity: multiple matches
1.text: Ambiguity: multiple matches. If a tool returns several customers with the same name, ask for an additional identifier (email, phone, order number). Do not pick one by a heuristic (most recent, most orders): a wrong guess exposes another person's data or refunds the wrong account. Exam tip: Sentiment thresholds and confidence cutoffs are classic wrong answers. The proportionate first step is explicit criteria plus few-shot examples. Exam tip: Several matching customers to ask for another identifier; never pick one by a heuristic.

1.title: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems
1.text: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems. Case (continued): The research subagent that searches the web times out on a hard topic. What should reach the coordinator?

1.title: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems, continued
1.text: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems, continued. The figure shows this: Structured error context for the coordinator: failure type, attempted query, partial results and possible alternatives.

1.title: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems, continued
1.text: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems, continued. Failure type (timeout, access denied, rate limited). Decides retry versus alternative. What was attempted (the exact query). Lets it retry with a changed query. Partial results. Work already done is not thrown away. Possible alternatives. Suggests another source or approach. Access failure versus valid empty result: a timeout needs a retry decision; a successful search with no matches is a legitimate answer. Generic statuses such as "search unavailable" hide the context the coordinator needs. Local recovery: the subagent retries transient failures itself and propagates only unresolved errors, with what was attempted and partial results.

1.title: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems, continued
1.text: Error Propagation in Multi-Agent Systems, continued. Silently suppressing errors (return an empty set marked successful). The failure is invisible; the report looks complete but is not. Terminating the whole workflow on one failure. Throws away everything that worked when recovery was possible. Coverage annotations: the final output should mark which findings are well supported and which areas have gaps because sources were unavailable. Exam tip: Best answer for a subagent failure equals structured error context to the coordinator, then recover or proceed with partial results and annotate gaps.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Escalate when: Explicit human request (immediately), policy gap or exception, no meaningful progress. Frustration only: Acknowledge, offer to resolve; escalate if the customer repeats the request. Bad proxies: Sentiment and self-reported confidence. Fix calibration: Explicit criteria plus few-shot examples in the system prompt. Multiple matches: Ask for another identifier; no heuristics. Error context: Failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives. Distinguish: Access failure (error, retry decision) versus valid empty result (success, none found). Anti-patterns: Silent suppression; abort everything. Recovery: Local retry of transient errors; propagate the unresolved; annotate coverage gaps.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Birchwood's agent escalates routine address changes but tries to settle gift-card disputes that need exceptions by itself. What is the best first improvement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The root cause is unclear decision boundaries; criteria with examples are the proportionate fix. Self-reported confidence is unreliable and a classifier is heavy infrastructure.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A customer writes: "I want to speak to a person." What should the agent do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. An explicit request for a human is honored at once.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A customer sounds irritated about a late parcel but does not ask for a person, and the agent can see the tracking and fix the issue. What is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Frustration alone is not an escalation trigger when the agent can resolve the issue.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A customer asks for a price match with a competitor's website, and the policy covers only adjustments to Birchwood's own prices. What should the agent do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A policy gap is a legitimate trigger for escalation.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A search for customer "Sam Rivera" returns three records. What should the agent do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. With multiple matches, request clarification rather than selecting by heuristic.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. The web search subagent times out. Which design best allows intelligent recovery? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Rich context lets the coordinator retry, change approach or proceed with partial results. A generic status hides it, an empty success hides the failure, and a total stop wastes working parts.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which statement describes a valid empty result? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. An empty result from a successful query is an answer; the others are failures.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Where should a final research report show that one region's data could not be retrieved? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Annotating coverage keeps the report honest about which areas are well supported and which have gaps.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two are valid reasons to escalate to a human? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. Explicit requests and policy gaps are real triggers. Tone, sentiment scores and self-reported confidence are weak proxies for difficulty.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all nine answers. Question one: D. Question two: A. Question three: A. Question four: B. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: A. Question eight: A. Question nine: A and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
